title: Auto Layout & Adaptive UI
summary: UIKit's constraint-based layout system as a system of equations, and adapting across iPhone and iPad screen sizes with size classes — plus the two mistakes that produce ambiguous or broken layouts.

slides.markdown:
Before Auto Layout, UIKit positioned views with hardcoded pixel frames — fine for one screen size, broken the instant a new device shipped. Auto Layout replaced that with **constraints**: relationships between views that a solver resolves into concrete frames, automatically, whenever the screen size, orientation, or content changes.

The mental shift is from 'here's the exact position' to 'here's the relationship, you figure out the position' — and that shift is exactly what makes one layout work correctly on an iPhone SE and an iPad Pro without writing separate code for each.

slides.sectionTitle: Constraints as a system of equations
slides.markdown:
Every constraint is literally a linear equation: `view1.attribute = multiplier × view2.attribute + constant`. "Pin this button's leading edge 16 points from its superview's leading edge" is `button.leading = superview.leading + 16`. Auto Layout's solver — Cassowary, the same constraint-solving algorithm used elsewhere in UI toolkits — gathers every constraint affecting a view and solves them simultaneously for the actual frame.

This framing explains a lot of Auto Layout's behavior that seems mysterious otherwise: if you provide **too few** equations, the system is under-determined and a view's position is ambiguous; provide **contradictory** ones, and the system is over-determined and something has to lose. Auto Layout doesn't guess — it resolves exactly what the math says, which is either exactly enough constraints, or a documented tie-breaking rule (priority) for the rest.

slides.subTitle: when each is simpler
slides.markdown:
| | UIStackView | Raw NSLayoutConstraint |
|---|---|---|
| Sequential rows/columns of views | trivial — just add subviews in order | verbose — pin each view's edge to the previous one |
| Dynamic show/hide of a subview | automatic re-layout via isHidden | manual constraint updates |
| Fine control over one specific relationship | limited (spacing, alignment only) | full control |
| Nesting for complex layouts | composable (stacks within stacks) | flat, harder to read |

`UIStackView` is itself built on Auto Layout underneath — it generates the constraints for you for the common case of 'lay these views out in a row or column.' The practical rule: default to a stack view for anything sequential, and drop to raw constraints only for the specific relationships a stack view can't express (an aspect ratio pin, a constraint between two views in different branches of the hierarchy).

```swift
NSLayoutConstraint.activate([
    contentView.leadingAnchor.constraint(
        equalTo: view.safeAreaLayoutGuide.leadingAnchor, constant: 16),
    contentView.trailingAnchor.constraint(
        equalTo: view.safeAreaLayoutGuide.trailingAnchor, constant: -16),
    contentView.topAnchor.constraint(
        equalTo: view.safeAreaLayoutGuide.topAnchor),
    contentView.bottomAnchor.constraint(
        equalTo: view.safeAreaLayoutGuide.bottomAnchor)
])
```

The **safe area** excludes the notch/Dynamic Island, home indicator, and status bar — pinning to `safeAreaLayoutGuide` instead of the raw view edges means content automatically avoids those regions on every device shape without device-specific code. Pinning to the plain `view` edges instead is the fastest way to get content clipped behind the Dynamic Island on newer iPhones.

slides.subTitle: adapting layout across iPhone and iPad
slides.markdown:
**Size classes** abstract away exact screen dimensions into a coarser signal: each dimension is either `.compact` or `.regular`. An iPhone in portrait is compact-width/regular-height; an iPad is regular-width/regular-height in most orientations; an iPhone in landscape (larger models) can be regular-width/compact-height.

Interface Builder lets you vary constraints, constants, and even whole subviews per size-class combination directly, and in code `traitCollectionDidChange` fires when a trait (including size class) changes — a device rotation, or a multi-window resize on iPad. Designing against size classes rather than specific device dimensions is what makes a layout survive the next device Apple ships without a code change, since the *next* iPhone is still compact-width in portrait even if its exact pixel dimensions are new.

A view with too few constraints to fully determine its frame is **ambiguous** — Auto Layout picks *some* valid frame satisfying the constraints it has, but which one is essentially unspecified and can differ between layout passes, leading to a view that visibly jumps or resizes for no apparent reason.

The fix is making sure every view has enough constraints to fully determine both its position (x, y) and size (width, height) — either directly, or transitively through its content (a label's intrinsic content size supplying width/height once its edges anchor it). Xcode's `View Debugger` and runtime console warnings ("Unable to simultaneously satisfy constraints") flag ambiguity directly — treat any ambiguous-layout warning as a bug to fix immediately, not noise to ignore, since the visible symptom can be intermittent and device-specific.

Setting a view's `frame` directly, or a constraint constant computed from a hardcoded screen width assumption (`UIScreen.main.bounds.width / 2 - 40`), reintroduces exactly the device-specific brittleness Auto Layout exists to remove. It works on the device it was tested on and silently breaks — overlapping content, off-screen elements — on any other size, including the *next* device model.

The fix is relative constraints (percentages via multipliers, or anchoring to layout guides) instead of absolute pixel math, and letting content-based sizing (intrinsic content size, `UIStackView` distribution) do the work instead of manually computing widths. If a genuinely device-specific tweak is unavoidable, gate it on size class or trait, not a raw pixel width comparison — the pixel width of 'iPhone in portrait' isn't stable across models, but its size class is.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior nuance: content hugging and compression resistance
slides.markdown:
A mid-level answer stops at 'add enough constraints.' A senior answer knows that when two views compete for the same space with no other tiebreaker, **content hugging priority** decides which one grows to fill extra space (lower hugging priority = more willing to grow) and **compression resistance priority** decides which one shrinks first under too little space (lower resistance = shrinks first).

The classic case: a `UILabel` next to a fixed-width icon in an `HStack`-equivalent row, where the label should absorb extra width and truncate under pressure while the icon stays fixed. Setting the icon's horizontal compression resistance higher than the label's is what actually enforces that — without it, both views are equally willing to shrink, and which one visually squishes first at layout time is left to Auto Layout's internal tie-breaking rather than the designer's intent. This is the mechanism behind most "why did my label truncate instead of my image shrinking" bugs.
